question.prompt: Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\) in regular tetrahedron \(ABCD.\) What is \(\cos(\angle CMD)?\)

solutions.title: Use triangle CMD
solutions.explanation:
The midpoint of an edge gives altitudes in two equilateral faces, so we can find all three sides of \(\triangle CMD\).

Scale the tetrahedron so that every edge has length \(2\). Since \(AC=BC\) and \(M\) is the midpoint of \(AB\), the median \(CM\) is perpendicular to \(AB\). Thus the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
CM=\sqrt{BC^2-BM^2}=\sqrt{4-1}=\sqrt3.
\]
The same argument in face \(ABD\) gives \(DM=\sqrt3\), while \(CD=2\).

In \(\triangle CMD\), the side opposite \(\angle CMD\) is \(CD\). Therefore the law of cosines yields
\[
\cos(\angle CMD)
=\frac{CM^2+DM^2-CD^2}{2(CM)(DM)}
=\frac{3+3-4}{2\sqrt3\sqrt3}
=\boxed{\frac13}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{B}\).

solutions.title: Project onto the opposite face
solutions.explanation:
Projecting \(D\) onto face \(ABC\) creates a right triangle containing the desired angle.

Let \(O\) be the foot of the perpendicular from \(D\) to the plane of \(ABC\). By the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
OA^2=DA^2-DO^2,
\quad OB^2=DB^2-DO^2,
\quad OC^2=DC^2-DO^2.
\]
Because \(DA=DB=DC\), we have \(OA=OB=OC\). Thus \(O\) is the circumcenter of the equilateral triangle \(ABC\). Its perpendicular bisectors are also its medians, so \(O\) is the centroid. A centroid divides each median in the ratio \(2:1\), with the longer part next to the vertex. Consequently, \(O\) lies between \(M\) and \(C\), and
\[
MO=\frac13 MC.
\]

The equilateral faces \(ABC\) and \(ABD\) are congruent, so their medians \(MC\) and \(MD\) have equal lengths. Also, \(DO\perp MO\), because \(DO\) is perpendicular to the entire base plane. Since rays \(MO\) and \(MC\) coincide, the right triangle \(MOD\) gives
\[
\cos(\angle CMD)
=\cos(\angle OMD)
=\frac{MO}{MD}
=\frac{MC/3}{MC}
=\boxed{\frac13}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
